summary: Describes GREASE, a mechanism to prevent extensibility failures in the TLS ecosystem. It reserves a set of TLS values that clients and servers may advertise so that peers keep correctly handling unknown values instead of breaking when new ones appear.

eli5.summary: If you never try new words, people forget how to cope with them. GREASE sends harmless made-up words so everyone stays used to unexpected ones.

questions: why does tls reserve random values
subtitle: Reserved TLS values that clients sprinkle into handshakes at random, so broken servers get caught before the protocol rusts shut.

tldr.problem: TLS depends on peers ignoring values they do not know. A bug that rejects unknown values can spread unnoticed, and then new values cannot be deployed without breakage.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves unused values for cipher suites, extensions, named groups, signature algorithms, versions, ALPN identifiers and PskKeyExchangeModes. Implementations MAY advertise them at random, and peers must treat them like any unknown value.
tldr.outcome: Peers that cannot tolerate unknown values fail early and visibly, so the mistake is found before it is widespread.

today: RFC 8701 is an Informational document from January 2020. No RFC obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the reserved GREASE values for TLS.

sections.title: The Rusted Joint Problem
sections.content:
TLS (RFC 8446) has several points of extensibility, including the list of cipher suites and several lists of extensions. One side, usually the client, advertises capabilities and the peer, usually the server, selects them. The responding side must ignore unknown values so that new capabilities can be introduced without breaking interoperability.

Bugs can make an implementation reject unknown values. Such an implementation still works with existing peers, so the mistake can spread unnoticed. When new values are later defined, the metaphorical joint in the protocol has rusted shut.

The fix is to reserve some currently unused values and have implementations advertise them at random. Correct peers ignore them and carry on. Peers that do not tolerate unknown values fail, which reveals the mistake early. The technique is called GREASE, short for Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility.
sections.eli5: A door hinge that is never moved gets rusty and stuck. Swinging the door a little every day keeps it working, and tells you early if something is wrong.

sections.title: The Reserved GREASE Values
sections.content:
The GREASE values were allocated sparsely to discourage servers from conditioning on them. They share a number pattern across all types and avoid collisions with existing TLS registries.

  • For cipher suites and ALPN identifiers there are sixteen two-byte values, from {0x0A,0x0A} to {0xFA,0xFA}, stepping the high nibble each time.
  • For extensions, named groups, signature algorithms and versions there are sixteen values from 0x0A0A to 0xFAFA.
  • For PskKeyExchangeModes there are eight values: 0x0B, 0x2A, 0x49, 0x68, 0x87, 0xA6, 0xC5 and 0xE4.

The reserved version values are thus no longer available as TLS or DTLS version numbers.
sections.eli5: The authors set aside a few special, never-used numbers, like putting fake coins in a game, that everyone agrees do not mean anything.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
In a ClientHello, a client MAY pick one or more GREASE values and advertise them in cipher_suites, as extensions with varying length and contents, and in supported_groups, key_share, signature_algorithms, signature_algorithms_cert, supported_versions, psk_key_exchange_modes and the ALPN extension. For a key_share entry, the key_exchange field MAY be any value.

Servers MUST NOT treat GREASE values differently from any unknown value, MUST NOT negotiate one, and MUST ignore unknown values and try the remaining parameters. Clients MUST fail the connection if a server selects a GREASE value, for instance in the ServerHello version or cipher suite or in a server CertificateVerify signature. The text notes that no special processing is needed, since the existing rule to reject unknown server-selected values already covers it.

Some extension points are offered by the server. In TLS 1.3 a server MAY add GREASE extensions and signature algorithms to a CertificateRequest, and GREASE extensions to a NewSessionTicket. The roles then mirror: clients must ignore them as unknown values, and servers MUST fail the connection if a client negotiates one, for example in a client CertificateVerify signature.
sections.eli5: The sender hides a few pretend items in a list. The receiver must skip them like any item it does not know, and must never choose one for real.

sections.title: Choosing When to Send GREASE
sections.content:
Implementations that advertise GREASE values SHOULD select them at random, which encourages peers to ignore all unknown values rather than one specific value. They MUST still follow the protocol rules. For example, RFC 8446 forbids duplicate extension types in one extension block, so several GREASE extensions in a block must use different values.

Implementations SHOULD also balance diversity with determinism. A client that varies GREASE positions on every connection may fail against a broken server only some of the time, and automatic retries can mask the failure. A client that positions GREASE deterministically over a period, such as a single software release, tests fewer cases but is more likely to catch bugs in them.
sections.eli5: Mix up which pretend items you hide, but not so wildly that a failure only shows up once in a blue moon and gets hidden by trying again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GREASE values cannot be negotiated, so they do not directly affect TLS security. Historically, when a new TLS feature caused interoperability problems, implementations retried with the feature disabled, which lets an active attacker silently turn the feature off. By preventing a class of such problems, GREASE reduces the need for this fallback. Implementations SHOULD NOT retry with GREASE disabled after a connection failure, since that would stop GREASE from defending against extensibility failures.

If GREASE values are not chosen at random, the implementation, or even individual users, could be fingerprinted, which harms privacy.
sections.eli5: If you always hide the same pretend items in the same spots, people can tell it is you by your habit. Picking randomly keeps you hard to spot.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content: The RFC adds the reserved values to four IANA registries: TLS Cipher Suites, TLS Supported Groups, TLS ExtensionType Values, and TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs. In each, the entries are marked Reserved with this RFC as the reference. In the three registries that carry a Recommended column, the value is N.
sections.eli5: The authors told the official list keeper to mark these numbers as reserved, so nobody uses them for something real by accident.
